newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal pilots warn TAP move a risk to safety.
newsitem.headline: Portugal pilots warn TAP move a risk to safety.

text.p: Pilots warned on Wednesday that loss-making national airline TAP-Air Portugal's attempt to make them fly more hours was a threat to passenger safety.
"This climate is affecting the psychological stability of pilots, which is indispensable to the security of flying," the pilots' union said in a statement.

Nearly 200 pilots, mainly those from long and medium haul flights, met in Lisbon after the company said it had asked the country's aviation authority to order an extension of flying hours over the busy summer period.
The company's request, which looked set to be granted, was the latest move in a long-running dispute with senior pilots over working hours.

TAP says its pilots work fewer hours than those of its major competitors and that the future of the company is at risk unless it wins reforms. Pilots say that the problem is due to poor organisation and reject any attempt to increase flying times.
The Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres on Saturday issued a special decree ordering pilots to end a series of selective strikes which were disrupting services.
But TAP has continued to cancel some flights as a number of pilots responded to the government order by calling in sick.
Some six flights were affected on Wednesday.

The Civil Aviation Pilots' Union (SPAC) said after the meeting that most of the 170 pilots present at the meeting, just under half the 430 pilots employed by the company, intended to ask company doctors to certify that they were psychologically fit for duty.

Recalling the last major plane crash in Portugal 20 years ago, which coincided with a moment of labour tension, pilots said that the government and airline management would be responsible for anything that could happen as a result of tiredness or stress.
The last major accident occurred in November 1977 when 129 people were killed at Funchal, in Portugal's Madeira islands, when a Boeing 727 skidded off the runway on landing.

"The pilots hold (Planning Minister) Joao Cravinho and the TAP management responsible for the consequences of any accident linked to tiredness or nervousness caused by this unjustified coercion," the pilots said in their statement.
The Director-General of Civil Aviation was expected to announce on Thursday whether he would agree to the TAP request for a temporary extension in working hours.
Both government officials and leaders of the pilots' union said that in the past such requests have been granted automatically.

TAP wants to raise the number of hours a pilot can fly each week to some 51 hours, from the present 45, and reduce the number of pilots that must be present on long haul flights from the current four.
The measure, if accepted, would remain in effect until the end of October. It is similar to the sort of reorganisation that the company has been seeking on long-term basis.
According to senior company officials, existing company regulations mean pilots work some 10 hours a week less than their colleagues at competitors such as Air France and Germany's Lufthansa.
